extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; legislators and those designing constitutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constituting and organizing a city-state: which offices, social arrangements, population size, geography, and moral ends a well-governed city should have so that citizens may live the happiest life. Emphasizes the relation between virtue, institutions, and the material/structural necessities of a polis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division and hierarchy of military command
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are horse and light-armed troops, and bowmen, and sailors, they sometimes put distinct commanders over each of these; who again have others under them, according to their different divisions; all of which join together to make one military body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize military command by arms and divisions with subordinate commanders so disparate forces form one cohesive body. Separate commanders may be appointed when forces (e.g., cavalry, archers, sailors) are present; in small cities a single general or polemarch may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial oversight officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Since some of the magistrates, if not all, have business with the public money, it is necessary that there should be other officers, whose employment should be nothing else than to take an account of what they have, and correct any mismanagement therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create dedicated fiscal officers whose sole charge is accounting and correcting mismanagement of public revenues and expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme magistrate with power to preside and summon
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one who is supreme over them all, who very often has in his own power the disposal of the public revenue and taxes; who presides over the people when the supreme power is in them; for there must be some magistrate who has a power to summon them together, and to preside as head of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an office (single magistrate or presiding official) empowered to convene the people and oversee public revenue; this role centralizes leadership and public assembly functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils / preadvisers
rubrics_metrics.description: These are sometimes called preadvisers; but where there are many, more properly a council. ... Amongst the magistrates also may finally be reckoned those who are to give their advice in public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use councils (many preadvisers) to advise and share responsibilities when appropriate; advisory bodies should be constituted to assist magistrates in public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicated religious officers and temple custodians
rubrics_metrics.description: There are other persons whose business is confined to religion; as the priests, and those who are to take care of the temples, that they are kept in proper repair, or, if they fall down, that they may be rebuilt; and whatever else belongs to public worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate priesthood and temple-keeping duties from secular magistracies; assign responsibility for sacred revenue, temple maintenance, and public worship to dedicated officers or groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers in charge of public sacrifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Next to these are those who are appointed to have the general care of all those public sacrifices to the tutelar god of the state, which the laws do not entrust to the priests: and these in different states have different appellations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign officers (distinct from priests) to oversee state public sacrifices when laws do not entrust those rites to priests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated public departments
rubrics_metrics.description: To enumerate in few words the different departments of all those magistrates who are necessary: these are either religion, war, taxes, expenditures, markets, public buildings, harbours, highways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the state has magistrates or administrative departments covering these core functions: religion, military affairs, taxation, public spending, markets/regulation, public works, ports, and roads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and custodial officers for courts and prisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Belonging to the courts of justice there are scribes to enroll private contracts; and there must also be guards set over the prisoners, others to see the law is executed, council on either side, and also others to watch over the conduct of those who are to decide the causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff courts with scribes, guards, execution officers, counsels, and oversight personnel to maintain legal process integrity and monitor judges' conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching magistracy forms to regime types
rubrics_metrics.description: As there are three magistrates to whom some states entrust the supreme power; namely, guardians of the laws, preadvisers, and senators; guardians of the laws suit best to an aristocracy, preadvisers to an oligarchy, and a senate to a democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the proper supreme magistracy structure compatible with the regime: guardians of the laws for aristocracy, preadvisers for oligarchy, and a senate for democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the best government by first determining best way of life
rubrics_metrics.description: He who proposes to make that inquiry which is necessary concerning what government is best, ought first to determine what manner of living is most eligible; for while this remains uncertain it will also be equally uncertain what government is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators must ground constitutional design in a prior, explicit account of the desirable way of life for citizens (the telos) — political arrangements should enable that life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary political aim: enable virtuous action and happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evident that government must be the best which is so established, that every one therein may have it in his power to act virtuously and live happily... a man's happiest life, both as an individual and as a citizen, is a life of virtue, accompanied with those enjoyments which virtue usually procures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitute government so individuals can practice virtue; prioritize institutional arrangements that foster moral and intellectual excellence over mere external goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods are limited; soul-virtues are central to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: For no one would say that a man was happy who had no fortitude, no temperance, no justice, no prudence ... every good quality of the soul the higher it is in degree, so much the more useful it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and constitutional choices should not place primary weight on wealth, honor, or power; evaluate states by their capacity to cultivate soul-virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: War as a means, not a final end
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evident therefore that the business of war is to be considered as commendable, not as a final end, but as the means of procuring it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design military policy to secure the conditions for the good life; avoid making conquest or domination the ultimate policy goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: City size judged by strength and order, not population alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Most persons think that it is necessary for a city to be large to be happy: but... they ought rather to consider its strength than its numbers... the perfection of a city consists in the largeness of it as far as that largeness is consistent with that order already mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set limits on city population so it remains governable and ordered; prefer a size sufficient for self-defense and self-sufficiency but small enough for magistrates to know citizens' characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper territorial extent and defensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: As to what soil it should be, every one evidently will commend it if it is such as is sufficient in itself to furnish what will make the inhabitants happy... It should be difficult of access to an enemy, but easy to the inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose territory and site that can supply necessary goods, is defensible, and facilitates internal ease of movement and defense; consider military geography and supply lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime position and regulated commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: If anything good arises from such an intercourse the city will receive it, but if anything hurtful, it will be easy to restrain it by a law declaring and deputing whom the state will allow to have an intercourse with each other... As to a naval power, it is by no means doubtful that it is necessary to have one to a certain degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate near the sea when advantageous, but regulate foreign intercourse and merchants by law so that maritime traffic benefits the city's needs rather than undermining laws or civic character; maintain an appropriate naval force based on the state's health and ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select citizen character: combine courage and prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Those persons ought to be both sensible and courageous who will readily obey a legislator, the object of whose laws is virtue... the Grecians... partake of them both as to be at the same time both courageous and sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to cultivate citizens who blend courage and practical intelligence so they can sustain freedom and civic life; consider education and customs that cultivate both qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honoring martial virtue and cultural norms regarding courage
rubrics_metrics.description: With some there are laws to heighten the virtue of courage; thus they tell us that at Carthage they allowed every person to wear as many rings for distinction as he had served campaigns... a law in Macedonia, that a man who had not himself killed an enemy should be obliged to wear a halter...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legal and customary honors to incentivize and recognize martial excellence, but be mindful of balance with virtue and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary material and institutional parts of a city
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the inhabitants must have food: secondly, arts, for many instruments are necessary in life: thirdly, arms... fourthly, a certain revenue... fifthly, which is indeed the chief concern, a religious establishment: sixthly... a court to determine both criminal and civil causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the polis can provide sustenance, necessary crafts/artisanry, defense forces, stable revenue, religious institutions, and judicial tribunals; these are indispensable for a functioning city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property necessary but not identical with the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Property is necessary for states, but property is no part of the state... a city is a community of equals, for the purpose of enjoying the best life possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize private property as essential for supporting social roles but not constitutive of the political community's identity; preserve commonality of civic ends over mere possessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division and exclusivity of employments for citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible that all may be common to all, or not, but only common to some... in democracies the whole community partakes of everything, but in oligarchies it is different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether roles (husbandmen, artificers, judges, counsellors) should be specialized or open to all; the choice shapes regime type and civic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of mechanical trades and commerce from full citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: In the best-governed states, where the citizens are really men of intrinsic and not relative goodness, none of them should be permitted to exercise any mechanic employment or follow merchandise, as being ignoble and destructive to virtue; neither should they be husbandmen, that they may be at leisure to improve in virtue and perform the duty they owe to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve full civic rights for those whose activities are 'noble' and allow others (slaves, servants, sojourners) to perform manual occupations; prioritize citizens' leisure for moral and political education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of soldier/senator/judge roles by capability and age
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to the employments of a soldier, a senator, and a judge... in some cases the same persons may execute them, in others they should be different, where the different employments require different abilities... what requires courage to the young, what requires judgment to the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign public roles according to natural aptitudes and life-stage: courage-oriented tasks to the young, judgment to the old; combine or separate offices based on whether required abilities coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landed property should belong to citizens intended for governance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also necessary that the landed property should belong to these men; for it is necessary that the citizens should be rich, and these are the men proper for citizens; for no mechanic ought to be admitted to the rights of a citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure land ownership among the governing citizen class to support their independence and suitability for civic duties; allow husbandmen (slaves, barbarians, servants) to work the land if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priesthood as a distinct, elder class
rubrics_metrics.description: The priests, for these evidently compose a rank by themselves; for neither are they to be reckoned amongst the husbandmen nor the mechanics... let the business of the priesthood be allotted to those who are in years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make religious offices distinct from economic and civic roles and assign them to elderly citizens to ensure reverence and continuity in worship practices.
